replying_to: Replying to Free Lunch Alignment of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models without Preference Image Pairs
display_title: Official Review of Submission4930 by Reviewer 6UbU

summary.value: This paper proposes Text Preference Optimization (TPO) for aligning text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models without human preference image pairs. It creates matched/mismatched text pairs via LLM-based prompt editing under four principles (content, attribute, spatial, contextual). Two variants, TDPO and TKTO, adapt DPO/KTO to diffusion training. Experiments across several benchmarks indicate consistent gains over Diffusion-DPO/KTO while remaining annotation-free.

strengths.value:
1. The idea of "free-lunch" alignment (re-using existing caption data + LLM perturbations) is creative, practical, and addresses real scalability issues in diffusion-model alignment.
2. The formulation of TDPO/TKTO directly mirrors established DPO/KTO objectives, but shifts preference comparison from outputs (images) to inputs (text prompts).
3. The method has been evaluated on four diverse datasets with multiple quantitative metrics. It achieves consistent improvement across most metrics and datasets. Qualitative comparisons convincingly show better text-image faithfulness, and ablation studies on editing principles and implicit-preference correlation provide solid analytical depth.

weaknesses.value:
1. The pipeline is essentially "synthetic preference data + existing DPO/KTO objective." Although effective and creative, it feels more like an engineering simplification than a fundamentally new learning principle.
2. The framework depends on a single budget-constrained LLM for prompt editing, which may introduce stylistic or semantic biases and restrict negative-sample diversity.

questions.value:
1. Can authors please clarify how LLM-generated and human-labeled prompts compare in alignment performance, possibly via a short correlation or qualitative analysis. This would clarify whether TPO truly approximates human alignment behavior or just benefits from larger-scale synthetic coverage.
2. I have concerns with the dependence on LLM prompt quality. Alignment quality is tied to how well the Gemini 2.0 Flash edits produce meaningful yet challenging negatives. Are there any quantitative analysis of negative-sample diversity?

> W2 \& Q2: The framework depends on a single budget-constrained LLM for prompt editing, which may introduce stylistic or semantic biases and restrict negative-sample diversity. I have concerns with the dependence on LLM prompt quality. Alignment quality is tied to how well the Gemini 2.0 Flash edits produce meaningful yet challenging negatives. Are there any quantitative analyses of negative-sample diversity?
    
**R2:**
We thank the reviewer for raising this interesting and important question.
In practice, we find that prompt editing is a relatively easy task, where a budgeted LLM already performs well at producing fine-grained and high-quality prompt modifications. Our quantitative results in table 1 and 2 suggest that the proposed method works effectively under such a budgeted LLM. At the same time, we agree with the reviewer that the capability and style of the LLM can influence the quality/diversity of the synthetic dataset and, consequently, the alignment behavior of TPO.

Taking this concern seriously, we plan to empirically examine the impact of LLM choice. Specifically, we will include an ablation using two additional LLMs of different capacities, qwen3-30b-a3b-instruct-2507 and llama-3.1-8b-it. LLM arena indicates a general capability of llama-3.1-8b-it < qwen3-30b-a3b-instruct-2507 $\approx$ gemini-2.0-flash. For each model, we (1) regenerate the modified prompts (2) compare the diversity within the modified prompts (3) rerun finetuning.

~~Due to limited computational resources, the experiment is still ongoing.~~

**R2.1** To answer your first question about LLM's capabilities' effect on final performance,
We show the performance comparison of using these three models for generating negative prompts as follows.

**Dataset: Pick-a-Pic**

| Method | Rewriting LLM         | PS    | CLIP  | HPS   | Image Reward |
|--------|------------------------|-------|-------|-------|--------------|
| SFT    | –                      | 71.20 | 50.80 | 62.00 | 72.80        |
| DiffusionDPO| -  | 72.80 | 54.20 | 52.40 | 68.60 |
| TDPO   | Gemini-Flash-2.0       | 75.20 | 56.00 | 69.20 | 82.60        |
| TDPO   | Qwen3-30b-a3b-it       | 75.20 | 54.80 | 64.40 | 78.40        |
| TDPO   | Llama-3.1-8b-it        | 68.20 | 54.00 | 61.00 | 72.80        |


**Dataset: Parti-Prompt**

| Method | Rewriting LLM         | PS    | CLIP  | HPS   | Image Reward |
|--------|------------------------|-------|-------|-------|--------------|
| SFT    | –                      | 69.06 | 52.38 | 63.31 | 73.81        |
|DiffusionDPO| - | 71.06 | 54.06 | 49.94 | 64.88|
| TDPO   | Gemini-Flash-2.0       | 74.63 | 57.25 | 70.19 | 78.75        |
| TDPO   | Qwen3-30b-a3b-it       | 72.19 | 54.94 | 65.19 | 76.25        |
| TDPO   | Llama-3.1-8b-it        | 67.44 | 54.00 | 64.44 | 75.81        |

It can be seen that Gemini-Flash-2.0 produces the best performance followed by Qwen3-30b-a3b-it. Llama-3.1-8b-it fails to provide meaningful improvements over the supervised-finetuning baseline. This suggests that the general capability of the LLM has a non-negligible impact on the final alignment performance. Notably, open-source alternatives such as Qwen3-30b-a3b-instruct are sufficiently powerful to deliver improvements over the baseline methods.


**R2.2** To further investigate the cause and answer your second question about negative sample quality, we furhter investigate the difference between the negative samples generated by different rewritting llms.

| Metrics | Gemini-Flash  | Qwen3 | Llama |
|-|-|-|-|
| Performance(Average) | 70.5 | 68.3 | 64.7|
| Prompt Difference(Edit Distance)| 2.8 | 8.4 | 19.3 |
| Diversity(Edit Distance)| 4.9 | 13.2 | 20.1 |
| Base model Implicit Preference Score $(10^{-5})$ | 5.2  | 6.5  | 12.6  |

As shown in the table above, prompt difference measures the average edit distance between the negative prompt and the original prompt, while negative diversity is computed as the mean pairwise edit distance among negative prompts within each group. Interestingly, we observe a negative correlation between performance and prompt difference—models that produce smaller edits to the original prompt tend to achieve higher performance. Since this trend is not intuitive, we further examine the corresponding Implicit Preference Scores of the prompt pairs on the base model. 

**We find that better-performing LLMs with lower edit distances consistently exhibit lower Implicit Preference Scores on T2I base model(sd 1.5). This means the T2I base model has a harder time telling the prompts apart, suggesting that these LLMs generate more nuanced, fine-grained modifications and that this subtlety is associated with improved downstream performance.**

comment.value:
> Q1: Can authors please clarify how LLM-generated and human-labeled prompts compare in alignment performance, possibly via a short correlation or qualitative analysis. This would clarify whether TPO truly approximates human alignment behavior or just benefits from larger-scale synthetic coverage.

**R3:**
We interpret the question as asking whether human annotators could produce negative prompts, and how our synthetically generated negatives compare to such human-modified negative prompts. 
Firstly, We would like to clarify that, in our work, **“human alignment behavior” refers to human preferences over images given a single prompt**. DiffusionDPO and DiffusionKTO require human-annotated image pairs conditioned on the same prompt, whereas our method utilizes synthetically generated text prompts. As shown in Table 2 and Figures 7 and 8, our Implicit Preference Score (see Section 4.3), is positively correlated with established human preference metrics (HPS, PS) trained from human-annotated image pairs. **This shows that our TPO aligns the model better to human preference.**

Secondly, At the same time, there are several issues for training with human-labled prompts:
* It is practically challenging to collect a sufficiently large and diverse set of human-written negative prompts.
* When humans are instructed to create negative prompts, they tend to be less creative and often produce only trivial modifications. Training on such low-quality modifications does not necessarily lead to performance improvement, especially since the original model is already strong enough to distinguish these simple changes.

Here we show a qualitative example where we asked human subjects to modify a prompt following our editing principles:

```
Original_prompt = Waterfall cascading down a cliff forms an elephant's likeness in verdant surroundings, flowing into a river bordered by large stones beneath the filtered sunlight
Human 1 Modification: elephant -> dog
Human 2 Modification: river -> sea
Human 3 Modification: large stones -> small stones
LLM Modification 1: verdant surroudning -> lush surrounding
LLM Modification 2: bordered by large stones ->  bordered by pebbles
LLM Modification 3: beneath the filtered sunlight -> beneath soft morning light.
```
We can see that LLM-based prompt edits tend to produce finer-grained, higher-quality modifications, whereas human edits are often limited to simple object or attribute substitutions.

> W1: The pipeline is essentially "synthetic preference data + existing DPO/KTO objective." Although effective and creative, it feels more like an engineering simplification than a fundamentally new learning principle.

**R1:** We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern and appreciate the perspective. Traditionally, aligning a generative model to human preferences requires the costly and time-consuming collection of human preference data. In contrast, our method provides a new alignment pathway that does not rely on any human preference supervision. While our approach indeed combines synthetic preference data with existing DPO/KTO objectives, we respectfully argue that this is more than an engineering simplification: it introduces a new paradigm for text-to-image alignment. By leveraging any high-quality image–caption dataset to construct synthetic text pairs, our method can, in principle, be scaled up much more efficiently. We see this scalability as a key advantage and an exciting direction for future work.

weaknesses.value:

The training recipe of TPO could potentially boost the similarity of the generations and the CLIP embedding and hence significantly improves performance on these related metrics. display_title: Official Review of Submission4930 by Reviewer PZtZ

summary.value: This paper introduces Text Preference Optimization (TPO), a framework to align text-to-image diffusion models without requiring human-annotated image preference pairs. The method uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate mismatched text prompts from original captions, creating text preference pairs (matched vs. perturbed) to train the model. The authors extend DPO and KTO to TDPO and TKTO, claiming state-of-the-art results on benchmarks like HPSv2 and Pick-a-Pic. While the core idea of "free lunch" alignment is novel, the paper's claims are significantly undermined by critical flaws in the experimental setup and evaluation.

strengths.value:
1. Original Idea: The concept of aligning models via automatically constructed text preferences, rather than image preferences, is novel and creative.
2. Practical Motivation: The work tackles a key scalability bottleneck in T2I alignment, offering a potentially cost-effective solution.
3. General Framework: The approach is model-agnostic and can be integrated with various preference optimization algorithms (DPO, KTO), which is a strong design choice.

weaknesses.value:
- Unconvincing Baseline Performance: The dramatic drop in performance for the Diffusion-DPO baseline (e.g., HPS score) is a major red flag. It suggests either a flawed implementation, inappropriate hyperparameters, or an unfair comparison setup, which invalidates the claimed superiority of the proposed methods.
- Opaque Training Process: The paper provides no insight into the training dynamics. There are no loss curves, convergence plots, or monitoring metrics on held-out benchmarks. This makes it impossible to assess if the models are learning the intended preferences or if the training is stable.
- Potentially Unfair Comparison: The baselines (Diffusion-DPO/KTO) are designed for human image preferences. Comparing them against a method using synthetic text preferences, where the negatives are generated by the same LLM pipeline, may not be a fair or meaningful comparison. The paper should have included a baseline using the same synthetic text to generate a negative image for a more controlled comparison.

summary.value:
This paper proposes a method, called text preference optimization (TPO), for aligning T2I diffusion models without requiring human-annotated image preference pairs. It uses a LLM to generate text prompts that do not match the original caption, thus, creating text preference pairs (accepted/rejected), and then uses them with LLM-based alignment algorithms, such as DPO and KTO. 

- The idea of starting without preference data and then using a LLM to generate preferred and dispreferred text prompts is very simple. However, the method would be biased towards the LLM generating matched/mismatched text prompts and its overall performance would heavily depend on the quality of the LLM. I also believe it is too strong to call such a method "free lunch alignment". The reviewers have the same concern about the effect of the LLM and view the work more like an engineering simplification than a fundamentally new learning principle.

- The reviewers also have major concerns regarding the experimental setup and results. 

- Finally, the idea is not novel either. A similar approach was used in "Confidence-aware Reward Optimization for Finetuning Text-to-Image Models (ICLR-2024)" to generate prompts that are synthetically similar but semantically different than the original caption. Of course, the resulting data was used to calibrate different reward scores to address reward hacking in T2I RLHF. 

As a result, I do not think the paper carries enough novelty and requires major improvements.

reviewer_concerns.value: I do not think the main concerns of the reviewers, especially Reviewers PZtZ and 6UbU, were addressed, because they are mainly related to the lack of novelty in the main contributions of the paper.

reviewer_scores.value: Unfortunately, none of the reviewers reacted to the authors' response. However, I doubt any of them would have changed their score, because their main concerns are related to the simplicity and the lack of novelty in the main contributions of the paper.
